## Question 85 (Year: 2013 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2013-gs3-q85-unacademy**
**Q1.With a consideration towards the strategy of inclusive growth, the new companies bill, 2013 has indirectly made CSR a mandatory obligation. Discuss the challenges expected in its implementation in right earnest. Also discuss otherprovisionsinthebillandtheirimplications. (150 Words, 10 Marks). Tag: Inclusive growth and issues arising from it. Indian economy and issues related to planning, mobilization of resources, growth development and employment.**

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In Intro try to write about Companies Bill** **2013 and CSR in brief.**-**In Body,**-**Discuss in brief provisions of the bill.**-**Discusses expected challenges in its** **implementation.**-**Discuss implications of the bill.**-**Try to conclude, answer by underlining the** **importance of the bill and CSR.** **Answer:**The Companies Act, 2013 regulates the incorporation, functioning, appointments of directors in board of directors, and dissolution of all types of companies. The Companies Act 2013 replaced the 1956 Companies Act. The of the Companies**section 156** Act 2013 talks about mandatory Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), making it the only law in the world which made mandatory CSR contributions.
- **Corporate social responsibility (CSR)** is a selfregulating business model that helps a company be socially accountable—to itself, its stakeholders, and the public.
- By practicing corporate social responsibility, also called corporate citizens, companies can be conscious of the kind of impact they are having on all aspects of society, including economic, social, and environmental.
- To engage in CSR means that, in the ordinary course of business, a company is operating in ways that enhance society and the environment, instead of contributing negatively to them.

## **Provisions of the Companies Act 2013**

- **Independent Directors:** Companies Act made mandatory that one-third members comprise independentdirectorsandatleast1womenshould be there as independent director.
- **Executive’s salary:** The new act says companies should disclose executive salaries as average employers’ salaries and this act also allows shareholders to file a class action lawsuit in case of violation of this section.
- **CSR Committee:** As per act companies need to set up a CSR board committee, which must consist of three directors and one of them should be independent director.
- **CSR contribution:** The Companies Act made mandatory that companies must spend an average 2% of net profit made in immediately preceding three financial years on CSR activities. Requirement of CSR will only apply to those companies which are incorporated in India, with net profit of 50 million or more.
- **Definition of CSR:** As per the act CSR activities are those acts which promote poverty reduction, environmentalsustainability,education,vocational skill development, and gender equity. Etc.
- **Positive step:** India is a country where one third populations is illiterate, two third population lacks sanitation, at least 100 million population still lives on less than $2 dollars/ day, the enactment of company’s act should be hailed as positive step towards ensuring equality and justifying article 39 and 40 of the Indian constitution.

## **Challenges In Implementation Of New Act**

- **Attitude of Corporates:** Most crucial is an attitude of big corporates, as foremost companies having been compulsorily required to comply with the Act, CSR is being perceived as an expenditure and not much attention having been paid to include the same as a part of actionable business agenda practices.
- **At Ground Level Companies** should be involved in CSR implementation and the route of only disbursing donations to NGOs or Trusts and remainingasilentspectatorshouldnotbethecase.
- **Attitude of Companies:** Companies still consider CSR contribution as a philanthropic gesture rather than considering CSR as a holistic view of the impactofbusinessontheenvironmentandsociety.
- As companies are **No Focus on Outcome:** looking at CSR just from a philanthropic point of view, they are not interested in looking at actual implementations of work and effectiveness of money and no focus on what outcome they are achieving through CSR activities in various areas.
- **High Level Committee:** The High-Level Committee [HLC] framed by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs in its report has mentioned that HLC has been suggested not to take actions against companies, at least for the initial two to three years for non-compliance of CSR provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
- **Women Independent Director:**the provision related to appointment of women independent directors has not been implemented seriously and there are very negligent women present in companies’ board of directors. Looking to the present social strata of the Country and a dire need for the balanced growth of the country, there needs a broader vision by moving ahead from the triple bottom line**“People, Planet** **andProfit”to“Partnership,ProgressandProsperity”.** CSR is need of an hour so as to contribute to the social innovation and development in India. India is the first and only country across the globe having mandatory enforcement of provisions relating to CSR for certain corporate entities vide Companies Act, 2013.

## Question 86 (Year: 2013 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Q 2. What are the reasons for introduction of Fiscal responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) act, 2003? Discuss critically its salient features and their effectiveness. (150 Words, 10 Marks). #

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In Intro try to write in brief about FRBM act.**-**In Body,**-**Discuss purpose and objectives of FRBM** **act 2003.**-**Discuss the utility and failure of the Act**-**Try to conclude your answer by mentioning** **the NK Singh committee.** **Answer:**The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act was enacted in 2003 which set targets for the government to reduce fiscal deficits. In 2016, the government set up a committee under**NK Singh**to review the FRBM Act. The government believed the targets were too rigid. The committee recommended that the government should target a fiscal deficit of 3 percent of the GDP in the years up to March 31, 2020, cut it to 2.8 per cent in 2020-21 and to 2.5 per cent by 2023.**The purpose and objectives of the acts can be** **understood in the following manner.** It seeks to foster fiscal discipline in the Central Government and achieve a balanced budget with effective revenue management. The objective of FRBM Act was to inculcate the habit of fiscal discipline in the governance. It fixes targets and suggests means of reducing fiscal and revenue deficits.

## **Objectives Under The Act**

- Reduction and Elimination of revenue deficit by 2008-09. Thereafter, build up adequate revenue surplus.
- Reduction of fiscal deficit to no more than 3 percent of GDP at the end of 2008-09.
- Reduce the Gross Fiscal Deficit (GFD) by March 31, 2008.
- Institutionalise India’s financial discipline.
- Improving macroeconomic management.
- Bring transparency in fiscal management of the country.
- To introduce more equitable and manageable debt over the years.
- The act aims to bring fiscal stability in India over the long run and additionally gives necessary flexibility to RBI to control inflation. The Central government shall lay in each financial year before both houses of Parliament the following statements of fiscal policy along with the annual

## **financial statement and demands for grants**

- The Medium-term Fiscal Policy Statement.
- The Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement.
- The Macro-Economic Framework Statement. **The utility of the Act** can be understood as it has given a framework within which the government has to outline and manage its fiscal deficit. Keeping fiscal deficit within a given target will improve confidence withinIndianeconomyandincreaseinvestmentwhich further boosts economic growth. Fiscal deficit is one of the very important economic tools which decides countries credit sovereignty in the global economy.
- **Unstable Targets:** However, the targets set under the original act have been periodically changed or amendmentmadewithintheactduetounforeseen conditions. For example, the 2008-09 subprime crisis government revised targets under the act and successive governments have failed to achieve the targets of fiscal deficit under act.
- **Debate on feasibility of the Act:** After 17 years of enactment of the Act there is debate whether the Government of India should continue with the target or not.
- One group is against setting Fiscal Deficit targets, as India is a developing nation and it needs to spend a lot of money on creating social and capital assets which are prerequisite for growth and development. The upper ceiling on expenditure of the government will force the Government to reduce spending.
- The opposite group which is in favour of the FRBM Act argued that missing the targets will lead to higher unnecessary targets, inflation, increased burden of debt and facing several other micro economic problems.
- **Infrastructure and SDGs:** Spending on social infrastructure to create productive assets are necessaryformIndia’stargettoachieveSustainable Development Goals and improve ranking in Human Development Index. But criticism is that the act prohibits the Government from higher spending.
- **Agriculture and Monsoon:** The vagaries of monsoon and one of the largest dependent populations on agriculture and over optimistic suggestions of the task force, which is in-charge of development of the target, highlighted some of the potential’s failures of the act. Hence, following fiscal targets and increasing social spending is the need of the hour. As NK Singh committee underlines that there are problems in setting up fiscal deficit targets in external situations or pandemic like situations. For example, in the 2020-21 financial year, the government has to borrow more for social sector spending like under various programmes of ATMA NIRBHAR BHARAT Abhiyaan.

Though the Indian Constitution does not have any explicit provision regarding right to food, the fundamental right to life enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution may be interpreted to include the right to live with human dignity, which can include the right to food and other basic necessities.

## **Eliminate Hunger and Malnutrition**

- TheNFSA2013requirestheexistingFoodSecurity policies of India into Laws. Example, the Mid Day Meal Scheme, Public Distribution System, the Antyodaya Anna Yojana, etc. are expanded and include provisions for reducing food deficiency in parts of India.
- **Right Based Approach:** NFSA has now changed the food security approach from welfare to right based which underlines right to food as a basic human and fundamental right, though the constitution has not declared the right to food as a fundamental right.
- **Coverage:** The Act legally entitled upto 75% of the rural population and 50% of the urban population to receive subsidized food grains under Targeted Public Distribution System. About two thirds of the population therefore is covered under the Act to receive highly subsidized food grains.

- **Special Provisions:** Wherein special provisions have been made for pregnant women and lactating mothers and children in the age group of 6 months to 14 years, by entitling them to receive nutritious meal free of cost through a widespread network of Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) centres, called Anganwadi Centres under ICDS scheme and also through schools under Mid-Day Meal (MDM) scheme.
- **Cash Incentives:** Higher nutritional norms have been prescribed for malnourished children upto 6 years of age. Pregnant women and lactating mothers are further entitled to receive cash maternity benefits of not less than Rs. 6,000 to partly compensate for the wage loss during the period of pregnancy and also to supplement nutrition.
- **Food Allowance:** In case of non-supply of the entitled quantities of food grains or meals to entitled persons under NFSA, such persons shall be entitled to receive such food security allowance from the concerned State Government to be paid to each person.
- **Grievance Redressal Mechanism:** To be set up at the District and State levels.

- Burden on the government.
- the World Trade Organization rules related issues.

- Exclusion error and inclusion error.

- Computerization of such shops in remote areas with no electricity and internet facilities. Since 2013, controversy has swirled around India’s National Food Security Act (NFSA), the most ambitious food security initiative in the world, with its plans to buy food grains from small-scale farmers to distribute to some 840 million poor Indians, twothirds of the country’s people. The controversy came at the World Trade Organization (WTO), where the U.S. government accused India of unfairly subsidizing its farmers by paying a support price above market prices. ## Question 94 (Year: 2013 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2013-gs3-q94-unacademy**
**Q 10. Discuss the rationale for introducing the Goods and services tax in India. Bring out critically the reasons for the delay in roll out for its regime. (150 Words, 10 Marks). Tag: Indian economy and issues related to planning, mobilization of resources, growth development, and employment. Government budgeting.**

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

The GST is paid by consumers, but it is remitted to the government by the businesses selling the goods and services.

## **Rationale Behind GST introduction**

- **The Complex Tax Structure:** The main reason behind the introduction of GST is simplifying tax structure. As there were many taxes imposed by States and Central governments which had a burden on taxpayers.
- **Improving Compliances:** Too many taxes discourage people and mainly industries to pay taxes. One nation one tax has decreased pressure of compliance of tax laws and made easier tax filing process and compliance to tax laws.
- **Increase Tax Revenue:** Increased tax revenue has become possible after the introduction of GST as the number of taxpayers increased. The government, both state and centre, are looking forward to making needed amendments to improve tax revenue.
- **Decrease Cascading Effects:** The ultimate burden of paying tax goes on citizens hence It was speculated that cascading effects or cascading burden of paying taxes on citizens. This reduced burden again helps increase taxpayers’ base.
- **Improve Fiscal Federalism:** As per GST law centre will pay compensation in case states would fail to get the expected amount of tax. This principle underlines fiscal federalism and also cooperative federalism for national development.
- **Destination Based Tax:**GST is destination-based hence this destination-based tax reduces paying multiple taxes on a single product has ended. ThoughGSTwasintroducedin2017ithasseenmultiple delays to introduce it. The delay of GST introduction can be understood by the following timeline.**Reasons Behind its Delayed Rollout:** The idea of a Goods and Services Tax (GST) for India was first mooted sixteen years back, during the then Prime Minister. The Empowered Committee (EC) of State Finance Ministers, which had formulated the design of State VAT was requested to come up with a roadmap and structure for the GST.
- **Difficulties of consensus building and charting**

## **out of technical difficulties took time**

- Based on discussions, the EC released its First Discussion Paper (FDP) on GST in November 2009. The FDP spelt out the features of the proposed GST and has formed the basis for the present GST laws and rules.
- In 2011, Constitution (115th Amendment) Bill, 2011 was introduced in the Lok Sabha to enable the levy of GST. However, due to a **lack** **of political consensus,** the Bill lapsed after the dissolution of the 15th Lok Sabha3.
- In December 2014, the Constitution (122nd Amendment) Bill 2014 was introduced in the Lok Sabha and was passed by Lok Sabha in 2015.
- Thereafter, the Constitutional Amendment Bill was moved on in 2016 based on political consensus. Finally, the Constitutional Amendment paved the way for the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax in India.
- Following this, State Legislatures of different States have passed respective State Goods and Services Tax Bills. However, Goods and Services Tax has been proving how it is significant but certain challenges need to be addressed. As recently the controversy created on GST compensation is an example of its implementation challenges, also their revenue shortages have been experienced as many times as possible a revenue collection is not steady, issues in tax filing, fake billing of GST, E-billing, etc need to be addressed to improve tax revenue, seamless and very easy way of taxcompliance,etc. If Indiawants to make OneNation One Tax a true game-changer and milestone in India’s tax administration, the implementation of GST at the ground level needs to improve.

## Question 95 (Year: 2013 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2013-gs3-q95-unacademy**
**Q 12. Adoptation of the PPP model for infrastructure development of the country has not been free from criticism. Critically discuss the pros and cons of the model. (250 Words, 15 Marks). Tag: Investment models. Indian economy and issues related to planning, mobilization of resources,growthdevelopment,andemployment.**

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In Introduction, define the concept of PPP.**-**In Body,**-**In the first part of the answer discuss the** **pros and;**-**In the second part of the answer, discuss** **the cons of PPP.**-**Conclude your answer with the underlying** **need for PPP.** **Answer:** Public-private partnerships involve collaboration between a government agency and a private-sector companythatcanbeusedtofinance,build,andoperate projects, such as public transportation networks, parks, and convention centers. Financing a project through a public-private partnership can allow a project to be completed sooner or make it a possibility in the first place. Public-private partnerships often involve concessions of tax or other operating revenue, protection from liability, or partial ownership rights over nominally public services and property to the private sector for-profit entities.

## **Pros of the PPP model**

- **Advantages to Both Parties:** Partnerships between private companies and governments provide advantages to both parties. Advantages such as fasten project completions, involvement of the private sector will improve business opportunities for them also.
- **Newer Technologies:** Once the private sector is allowed or given work to complete, they bring all the available latest technologies to finish projects. Private-sector technology and innovation, for example, can help improve the operational efficiency of providing public services.
- **Competitive Economy:** The public sector, for its part, provides incentives for the private sector to deliver projects on time and within budget. In addition, creating economic diversification makes the country more competitive in facilitating its infrastructure base and boosting associated construction, equipment, support services, and other businesses.
- Ensure the necessary investments into the public sector and more effective public resources management.
- Ensure higher quality and timely provision of public services. Most investment projects are implemented in due terms and do not impose unforeseen public sector extra expenditures.
- A private entity is granted the opportunity to obtain a long-term remuneration. Private sector expertise and experience are utilized in PPP project implementation.
- Appropriate PPP project risk allocation enables to reduce the risk management expenditures. In many cases, assets designed under PPP agreements could be classified on the public sector balance sheet. Although there are certain advantages of PPP, it has been criticized widely as it has some cons as well-

## **Cons of PPP**

- Infrastructure or services delivered could be more expensive.
- PPP project public sector payments obligations postponed for the later periods can negatively reflect future public sector fiscal indicators.
- PPP service procurement procedure is longer and more costly in comparison with traditional public procurement.
- PPP project agreements are long-term, complicated, and comparatively inflexible because of the impossibility to envisage and evaluate all particular events that could influence future activity.
- The private partner may face special risks from engaging in a public-private partnership. Physical infrastructure, such as roads or railways, involves construction risks.
- If the product is not delivered on time, exceeds cost estimates, or has technical defects, the private partner typically bears the burden.
- In addition, the private partner faces availability risk if it cannot provide the service promised. A company may not meet safety or other relevant quality standards, for example, when running a prison, hospital, or school.
- Demand risk occurs when there are fewer users than expected for the service or infrastructure, such as toll roads, bridges, or tunnels, recently Tejas Train controversy, etc.
- Public-private partnerships also create risks from the general public’s and taxpayers’ point of view.
- Private operators’ partnership with the government may insulate them from accountabilitytotheusersofthepublicservice for cutting too many corners, providing substandard service, or even violating peoples’ civil/constitutional rights.
- At the same time, the private partner may enjoy a position to raise tolls, rates, and fees for captive consumers who may be compelled by law or geographic natural monopoly to pay for their services. Although PPP has been criticized for its negative fallouts, India needs a huge amount of investment. The Finance Minister announced her plans at the start of the year to launch $1.5 trillion in infrastructure spending over the next five years. These infrastructural needs can be fulfilled by private sector involvement on a large scale. If India wants to become $5 trillion by 2025, building world-class infrastructure is imperative and a prerequisite.
[Question ID: 2013-gs3-q95-unacademy]

The main purposeofthepatentsystemistoencourageinnovation and eventually result in technological development.**Indian Scenario:** The present Patents Act, 1970 came into force in the year 1972 and amended through the Patent(amendment)Act2005.TheAmendmenttothe

## **Act brought following changes**

- **Section 3(d)** was introduced and introduced pharmaceutical product patents in India for the first time.
- The Act 2005 defines what **invention** is and makes itclearthatanyexistingknowledgeorthingcannot be patented.
- The provision defines a **‘novelty’**standard which, along with**‘non-obviousness’ or ‘inventive** **step’ and industrial applicability,** are the three prerequisites for ‘patentability’.
- **“Discovery”essentiallyreferstofindingsomething**which already existed in nature but was unknown or unrecognised. The most recent case, Novartis AG v Union of India5 decided by the Supreme Court of India in 2013 where the case began in the year 1997 related to drug name**GLIVEC**which was slightly a different version of their 1993 patent for ANTI LEUKAEMIA drug. In this case the petitioner challenged the constitutionality of section 3(d) before the High Court at Madras.**The applicant in the present appeal contented on two**

## **issues**

- Section 3(d) of the Act is unconstitutional as it violates the provision of the TRIPS agreement.
- The Indian patent act doesn’t define the term ‘efficacy’ and provides unguided power on the Controller. Hence it is arbitrary, illogical and vague. **In response to the above contention the Court held**

## **that**

- The WTO’s Dispute Settlement provides the exclusive remedy and a comprehensive dispute mechanismforviolationofTRIPSAgreement.The High Court looked into the conflict between the international law and municipal law and decided that municipal law prevails in such conflict.
- The court also rejected the second contention and the court observed that “Efficacy means the ability to produce a desired or intended result. Hence, the test of efficacy in the context of section 3(d) would depend upon the function, utility or the purpose of the product under consideration.

## **Appraisal of the Decision**

## Question 97 (Year: 2013 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2013-gs3-q97-unacademy**
**Q14.WhatdoyouunderstandaboutFixedDoseDrug Combinations (FDCs)? Discuss their merits and demerits. ( 250 Words, 15 Marks) Tag: Awareness in the fields of IT, Space, Computers, Robotics, Nano-technology, Biotechnology and issues relating to Intellectual Property Rights.**

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In the intro try to define FDC’s.**-**In Body,**-**Write pros and cons (advantages and** **disadvantages of the FDCs) in two** **different parts of the answer.**-**Try to conclude, by writing about the ban of** **the government and related controversies** **and underline India’s drug as a cheap but** **effective drug maker image world over.** **Answer:** It is a mix of two or more therapeutic ingredients in a single dose. Many of the popular cough syrups, painkillers, topical medications, anti-diabetes drugs as wellasantibioticsinthemarkettodayareFDCsbrands. Fixed-dose combination drugs can help improve adherence to an HIV treatment regimen by reducing the number of pills a person must take each day. An example of FDC HIV drug is Atripla (a combination of efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate).

## **Merits of FDC’s**

- **Reduced Pill Burden:** Improved medication compliance by the pill burden of the patients. This will also improve drug delivery as all the needed doses are taken into one dose.
- **Reduced Mental Burden:** It also reduces the burden of keeping track of all the medicines, their time of taking, keeping related information in mind or remembering it is a very tedious task hence it will help patients release pressure from mind and take one pill and be assured.
- **Reduce Effects of Single Drug:** It is said that FDC’s help in reducing effects of single drugs or single dose on patients.
- **Simplifying Drug Regime:** FDC’s help in simplifying complex treatment drug regime and help in achieving desired results of drugs combination on patients.
- **Treatment of type two diabetes:** Four key benefits areidentifiedanddiscussedinsupportofFDCsfor treatment of patients with T2DM: Greater efficacy comparedwithhigherdosemonotherapy,Reduced risk of adverse reactions relative to higher dose monotherapy, Lower overall costs, and Improved medication concordance.

## **Disadvantages of the FDCs**

- **Unwanted drugs:** As fixed drug combinations involve more than 2 drugs this sometimes creates issues for patients who need only a single drug.
- **Cost:** Cost of FDCs are the most critical issue as it is considered costly and patients who are poor and considering taking FDC’s causes out of pocket expenditure.
- **Patent’s protection:** FDC’s are considered themselves unique in nature and this may create issues of patent as companies invest significant amounts of money in R&D. Combining different drugs and making FDCs can cause issues of patent and copyrights issues.
- **Adverse Impact:** The major disadvantage is identifying drugs in case of adverse impacts of drugs. These adverse impacts of drugs sometimes lead to negative health impacts and even it may cause death of patients. The controversy arose when the government banned these drugs due to criticism that these drugs may be dangerous to health. It is convinced a large part of the products sold as FDCs are “irrational” and lack “therapeutic justification”, besides risking the health of patients. The greater clarity on the issues is needed as it is related to public health and also it may harm India’s image as a cheap but good quality drug maker all over the world.

## Question 98 (Year: 2024 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2024-gs3-q98-unacademy**
**Q4.Explain the role of millets for ensuring health and nutritional security in India. (150 Words, 10 Marks)**

#

## Answer

## **Answer**

## **Introduction**

- **Millets (Shree Anna)**are a group of small-seeded grains often termed**Nutri-cereals or Dryland-** **cerealslikeSorghum(Jowar),PearlMillet(Bajra),** **Finger Millet (Ragi), etc.**- Their resilience in adverse climatic conditions and ability to grow in rain-fed regions makes them crucial for sustainable agriculture, especially in India,**where 60% of cultivated land is rain-fed.** **Body**

## **Nutritional Benefits**

- **Rich in Nutrients:** Millets are packed with essential nutrients, including proteins, dietary fibre, vitamins, and minerals like iron, calcium, and magnesium. They provide a balanced diet, especially for populations with limited access to diverse food sources.
- **Low Glycemic Index:**Millets have a low glycemic index, which helps regulate blood sugar levels, making them beneficial for people with**obesity,** **diabetes and lifestyle problems** to maintain healthy weight.
- **High Fibre Content:** The high fibre content in millets aids in digestion and helps prevent constipation, contributing to overall gut health.
- **Anti-oxidants:**Millets are**abundant in** **antioxidants and bioactive compounds,**which help combat oxidative stress and protect against**chronic diseases such as cancer.**-**Curing Malnourishment:**For populations at risk of**malnutrition, millets provide essential** **vitamins, including B-complex vitamins like** **riboflavin and niacin,** which are crucial for overall health and well-being.
<p align="center"><img src="images/unacademy_p53_img97.png" alt="Diagram" /></p>

## **Food Security**

- **Drought Resistance:** Millets are hardy and drought-resistant crops, making them suitable for cultivation in arid and semi-arid regions of India. Their resilience helps ensure food security in areas prone to climate variability.
- **Climate Adaptability:**In times of climate change, they are the most secure crops to small farmers as they are the hardiest, most resilient and**climate** **adaptable crops**-**Short Growing Season:** Millets have a shorter growing cycle compared to traditional cereals, allowing farmers to harvest more frequently and contribute to food availability throughout the year.
- **Low Input Requirements:** Millets require fewer chemical inputs, such as fertilisers and pesticides, compared to conventional crops like rice and wheat. This makes them a more sustainable choice for farmers and reduces the environmental impact of agriculture.
- **Biodiversity:** Cultivating millets contributes to agricultural biodiversity, which is crucial for maintaining ecosystem balance and resilience against pests and diseases.
- **Soil Health: Millets improve soil health as a part** **of a mixed cropping system**and enhance the**biodiversity of farms, further contributing to** **sustainable agriculture.** **Conclusion**-**Millets play a crucial role in addressing India’s** **health and nutritional security challenges,** **offering significant benefits through their high** **nutrient content, resilience to climate change,** **and sustainable cultivation practices.**-**The United Nations’ designation of 2023 as the** **International Year of Millets underscores the** **global importance of these grains in combating** **hunger and promoting sustainable agriculture.**- India launched the**Millet International Initiative** **for Research and Awareness (MIIRA)**to globally coordinate millet research, focusing on**food** **security, nutrition, and climate resilience. This** **initiative will foster international collaboration** **in millet research and development.** ---

## Question 99 (Year: 2024 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2024-gs3-q99-unacademy**
**Q14.Elucidate the importance of buffer stocks for stabilizing agricultural prices in India. What are the challenges associated with the storage of buffer stock? Discuss. (250 words, 15 Marks)**

#

## Answer

## **Approach**

- **Introduction:** Define buffer stocks and introduce their significance in India’s food security.
- **Body:** Discuss how buffer stocks stabilize prices and ensure food security and identify the main challenges related to maintaining and managing buffer stocks.
- **Conclusion:**Emphasize the need for efficient management of buffer stocks and monitoring mechanisms.**Answer:** **Introduction:**Bufferstocksrefertothereserveofessentialfoodgrains like wheat and rice maintained by the government to stabilize prices, ensure food security, and manage supply during emergencies. The**Food Corporation** **of India (FCI)** is the primary body responsible for managing buffer stocks in India.

## **Importance of Buffer Stock**

- **FoodSecurity:Bufferstocksarecrucialtoensuring**the availability of food grains for schemes like the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) and welfare initiatives like**PM POSHAN,** particularly for vulnerable sections of society.
- **Price Stability:** By regulating the supply of food grains in the open market, buffer stocks help control inflation and stabilize food prices, preventing sudden price surges due to unexpected supply-demand imbalances.
- **Crisis Management:** In situations like natural disasters, unexpected crop failures, or economic disruptions, buffer stocks act as a safety net to provide immediate relief without relying on international imports.
- **Support for Welfare Programs:** Buffer stocks ensure the continuous release of food grains for welfare schemes, addressing malnutrition, hunger, and food scarcity, especially in economically disadvantaged regions.

## **Challenges with Buffer Stock**

- **EconomicCostsandSubsidyBurden:Maintaining**buffer stocks involves high storage costs and subsidies. Delays in subsidy releases force the FCI to rely on**extra-budgetary resources (EBR)** like borrowing from the National Small Savings Fund (NSSF), affecting public finance stability.
- **Storage Inefficiencies:**Poor storage conditions, including inadequate maintenance of warehouses, often result in significant grain losses due to**heat,** **humidity, and pests,** leading to wastage and inefficiency.
- **RegionalDisparitiesinProcurement:Themajority** of food grain procurement is concentrated in North-Western states, causing economic benefits to be unevenly distributed. This neglects farmers in other regions, affecting overall agricultural diversity and equitable development.
- **Overstocking and Rotting of Grains:** Critics argue that the FCI often holds excess grain beyond the necessary buffer limits, leading to spoilage. This is due to the lack of a precise mechanism for estimating the required quantity.
- **Impact of Export and Global Events:**During events like the**Russia-Ukraine war,**the excessive export of wheat and rice led to a depletion of buffer stocks. This, combined with domestic food inflation, created a shortfall in reserves, highlighting the need for better monitoring and regulation.**Conclusion:** Maintaining buffer stocks is essential for ensuring food security and stabilizing agricultural prices in India. However, improving the efficiency of buffer stock management is crucial to minimizing wastage, reducing costs, and achieving balanced benefits across regions. Effective monitoring, mathematical modeling of supply and demand, and a regionally inclusive procurementpolicyarenecessarystepstooptimizethe roleofbufferstocksinIndia’sfoodsecurityframework.

## Question 100 (Year: 2023 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2023-gs3-q100-unacademy**
**Q3. How does e-Technology help farmers in production and marketing of agricultural produce? (10 Marks, 150 Words)**

#

## Answer

## **Approach**

- **Intro:** Briefly define e-technology in agriculture.
- Body: Role in Production, Role in Marketing, and Issue.
- **Way Forward/Best Practices:** Suggest practical solutions.
- **Conclusion:**Summarize impact.**Answer:** **Introduction:** E-technologyinagricultureintegratesICT,AI,IoT,and digital platforms to assist farmers in decision-making, resource use, and market access. It helps enhance productivity and ensures better price realization, aligning with the goals of Digital India and Digital Agriculture Mission 2021-25.

## **Role in Production**

- **Satellite advisory & soil health cards:** ISRObacked advisories and 23 crore distributed Soil Health Cards guide farmers in crop choice and nutrient application, reducing input misuse.
- **AI apps:** Mobile applications like Plantix detect pest and disease stress in crops, helping cut yield losses estimated at 15–20%.
- **Drone use:** Subsidized under the Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanization (SMAM), drones are now used for spraying pesticides and fertilizers, reducing labour costs and time.
- **IoT sensors:** Smart irrigation systems optimize water and fertilizer usage, increasing efficiency by 20–25%.
- **Kisan Suvidha app:** Offers real-time weather, input, and market updates to millions of registered farmers, aiding timely decisions.

## **Role in Marketing**

- **e-NAM & Agmarknet:** Covering 1,300+ mandis, these platforms provide price discovery and arrivals data, giving farmers better bargaining power.
- **ITC e-Choupal:** Reaches over 4 million farmers across 35,000 villages, offering direct buyer access and quality inputs at fair prices.
- **ONDC integration:** Thousands of FPOs are onboarded, allowing farmers to sell products online and diversify markets.
- **Mobile payments (UPI):** With 13 billion transactions monthly in 2024, UPI enables secure and instant settlement for produce sales.
- **Digital warehouses:** NABARD’s Warehouse Digitization Programme tracks inventory quality, enabling farmers to secure better loans and price realization.

## **Issues**

- **Digital divide:** Only 37% of rural households had internet access as per NFHS-5, creating adoption gaps.
- **Low literacy:** Lack of regional-language apps restricts usage among small and marginal farmers.
- **Infrastructure deficits:** Poor broadband and power supply in villages weaken digital platforms’ outreach.
- **Cost of devices:** Smartphones, drones, and IoT tools remain unaffordable for many smallholders.
- **Cyberfrauds:Risingonlinescamsanddatamisuse** erode trust in digital transactions.

## **Way Forward**

- **Expand BharatNet & 5G:** Connecting 6 lakh villages with high-speed internet will ensure universal access.
- **Digital literacy:** Regional-language training programmes can empower farmers to effectively use apps and portals.
- **Subsidies via FPOs:** Providing drones, IoT kits, and AI tools through FPOs will spread adoption equitably.
- **Public-private partnerships:** Scaling successful models like e-Choupal can widen reach and build trust.
- **Smart village models:**Adopting best practices from Estonia and integrating ICT into village ecosystems can ensure inclusivity.**Conclusion:**E-technology has enhanced both**production** **efficiency and market access** for Indian farmers. With better connectivity, literacy, and trust, it can transform agriculture into a modern, resilient, and profitable sector.

## Question 101 (Year: 2023 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2023-gs3-q101-unacademy**
**Q13. Explain the changes in cropping pattern in India in the context of changes in consumption pattern andmarketingconditions.(15Marks,250Words)**

#

## Answer

## **Approach**

- **Intro:** Define cropping pattern and its dynamic nature.
- **Consumption-driven changes:** How rising demand shapes crops.
- **Marketing-driven changes:** How MSP, exports, FPOs, contract farming, etc. influence.
- **Issues:** Challenges in diversification.
- **Way Forward:** Policy suggestions.
- **Conclusion:**Balanced closure.**Introduction:**Croppingpatternreferstothedistributionofcultivated area among various crops in a region at a given time. In India, cropping patterns have changed significantly due to**shifts in consumer demand, globalization,** **MSP policies, and modern marketing systems.**

## **Changes Driven by Consumption Pattern**

- **Shift towards high-value crops:** Rising incomes and urban lifestyles increased demand for fruits, vegetables,milk,andpoultry;farmersaregradually moving away from traditional cereals.
- **Protein-rich foods:** Growing demand for pulses, soybean, and oilseeds to address protein needs has led to higher acreage under these crops, especially after government promotion of pulses during shortages.
- **Processed food demand:** Expansion of food processing and poultry industries boosted demand for maize, tomato, and potato cultivation, diversifying cropping patterns in states like Bihar and Madhya Pradesh.
- **Health and nutrition trends:** Growing interest in organic produce and coarse grains like millets (declared “Shree Anna” in 2023) encouraged farmers to reintroduce traditional crops.
- **Regional diversification:** Punjab and Haryana, once dominated by wheat-paddy cycles, are slowly shifting towards maize, vegetables, and horticulture due to rising consumer demand and groundwater stress.

## **Changes Driven by Marketing Conditions**

- **MSP policy bias:** Assured procurement of wheat and rice has encouraged monocropping in Green Revolution states, while discouraging diversification.
- **Export orientation:** Global demand increased the share of basmati rice, spices, cotton, and horticultural exports (India is the largest exporter of spices).
- **Contract farming and FPOs:** Examples include PepsiCo’s potato contracts in Punjab and Maharashtra’s grape FPOs supplying export markets, giving farmers market assurance.
- **Cold storage and logistics:** Improved storage and transportation facilities have enabled production of perishable crops like bananas, grapes, and flowers at a commercial scale.
- **Digital markets (e-NAM, ONDC):** Online trading platforms offer transparent pricing and better reach, incentivizing farmers to grow cash crops for higher returns.

## **Issues**

- **Over-dependence on cereals:** Punjab and Haryana continue cereal monocropping, worsening water stress and soil degradation.
- **Price volatility:** Fruits and vegetables often face market crashes due to poor cold chain infrastructure.
- **Smallholder vulnerability:** 85% of farmers are small and marginal, facing high risks in diversification without price security.
- **Unequal diversification:** Eastern India remains rice-dominated due to weak infrastructure and low market connectivity.

## **Way Forward**

- **Revise MSP policy** to incentivize pulses, oilseeds, and millets for nutritional security and crop diversification.
- **Expand food processing and cold chains** to stabilizepricesofperishablehorticulturalproduce.
- **Strengthen FPOs and cooperatives** to help small farmers access larger markets and reduce risks.
- **Agro-climatic planning** to align cropping with soil,rainfall,andconsumerdemandineachregion.
- **Promote consumer awareness**of diversified diets, creating steady demand for alternative crops.**Conclusion:**Cropping patterns in India are gradually shifting from**cereal dominance to high-value horticultural** **and protein-rich crops,**reflecting both**changing** **consumption habits and evolving market structures.**With supportive reforms in MSP, infrastructure, and farmer institutions, this transition can enhance**farmer** **incomes, food security, and sustainability.** ---

## Question 102 (Year: 2023 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2023-gs3-q102-unacademy**
**Q14. What are the direct and indirect subsidies provided to farm sector in India? Discuss the issues raised by the World Trade Organization (WTO) in relation to agricultural subsidies. (15 Marks, 250 Words)**

#

## Answer

## **Approach**

- **Intro:** Briefly define farm subsidies.
- **Direct Subsidies:** Examples with explanation.
- **Indirect Subsidies:** Broader support categories.
- **WTO Issues:** Why India’s subsidies are contested.
- **Conclusion:**Balanced closure.**Answer:** **Introduction:**Farm subsidies are government transfers and concessions given to farmers to support production, reduce risks, and ensure food security.In India, subsidiesarecrucialasagricultureemploysnearly45%**of workforce** but contributes only ~18% of GDP.

## **Direct Subsidies**

- : Government bears the gap **Fertilizer Subsidy**between cost and sale price; in**2023–24, subsidy** **was ~₹1.75 lakh crore.**- : Distributed via PDS and NFSA,**Food Subsidy** providing cheap foodgrains to ~81 crore people.
- **Input Subsidies:** Support for seeds, pesticides, irrigation under schemes like PMKSY.
- **Direct Income Transfer: PM-KISAN** gives ₹6,000 annually to ~11 crore farmers.
- **Crop Insurance Subsidy:** Government shares premium under PMFBY to reduce farmer risk.

## **Indirect Subsidies**

- **Power Subsidy:** Free/cheap electricity for irrigation, especially in Green Revolution states.
- **IrrigationSubsidy:Canalirrigationwatersupplied** at rates much below cost.
- **Credit Subsidy:** Concessional crop loans at 4–7% interest.
- **Export/Transport Aid:** Freight support and export incentives for agricultural products.
- **Research & Extension:** Subsidized agricultural R&D through ICAR, KVKs, and agri-universities.

## **Issues Raised by WTO**

- **Trade-distorting subsidies:** Amber Box subsidies (MSP, fertilizer) must remain within 10% of value of production.
- **MSP concerns:** India’s MSP for rice and wheat allegedly exceeds the 10% cap, especially with public stockholding.
- **Export competitiveness:** Subsidies make Indian exports cheaper, hurting global competitors.
- **Transparency issues:** India often delays notifications of subsidy data.
- **Food security vs. trade rules:** India argues subsidies are essential for poverty reduction, conflicting with WTO’s free-trade norms.

## **Way Forward**

- **Rationalize subsidies:** Shift from input subsidies (likefertilizerandpower)todirectincomesupport to avoid distortion.
- **Promote investment:** Redirect savings into irrigation, storage, mechanization, and R&D for long-term farm productivity.
- **Strengthen WTO negotiations:** Build alliances with G-33 nations to push for food security flexibility in subsidy norms.
- **Improve transparency:** Timely reporting of subsidies and adoption of WTO-compliant measures can reduce disputes.
- **Encourage sustainable subsidies:**Promote eco-friendly support such as organic farming incentives, solar pumps, and micro-irrigation.**Conclusion:**India’s farm subsidies ensure**food security and** **livelihood protection**but face WTO scrutiny as tradedistorting. A balanced approach combining**domestic** **reforms with assertive multilateral negotiations** is essentialtosafeguardfarmerinterestswhilecomplying with global rules.

## Question 103 (Year: 2022 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2022-gs3-q103-unacademy**
**13. What are the main bottlenecks in upstream and downstream process of marketing of agricultural products in India ? (Answer in 250 words) 15 Marks Approach**

#

## Answer

- **Introduction:** Introduce with the theme around process of marketing of agricultural products in India .

## **Body**

- Mention the Upstream and downstream bottlenecks.
- **Conclusion:Concludetheanswermentioning**the way forward.**Answer:** **Introduction:** The marketing of agricultural products in India involves various processes, from the upstream stages of production to the downstream stages of distribution andconsumption.However,severalbottleneckshinder the smooth functioning of these processes, affecting farmers and consumers alike.

## **Body**

## **Upstream Bottlenecks**

a. **Inadequate Infrastructure:** Poor infrastructure, such as inadequate roads and storage facilities, hampers the efficient transportation and storage of agricultural products. This can lead to wastage, reduced shelf life, and higher costs for farmers and consumers. Example: Due to inadequate cold storage facilities, perishable produce like fruits and vegetables often suffer spoilage before reaching the market, resulting in significant losses for farmers.
b. **FragmentedLandHoldings:Smallandfragmented** land holdings make it challenging for farmers to achieve economies of scale and access modern agricultural technologies. This can lead to lower productivity and reduced bargaining power in the market. Example: Fragmented land holdings often result in low production levels and difficulties in adopting mechanisation, impacting the overall productivity of the agricultural sector.
c. **Lack of Market Information:** Farmers often lack access to timely and accurate market information, leading to uninformed decisions regarding crop choicesandpricing.Thisinformationgapcanresult in market inefficiencies and price fluctuations. Example: Without real-time market information, farmers may not be aware of prevailing prices, leading to situations where they may sell their produce at lower rates than the market value.

## **Downstream Bottlenecks**

a. **Middlemen and Commission Agents:** The presence of multiple intermediaries, such as middlemen and commission agents, can lead to price distortions and reduced returns for farmers. These intermediaries often command a significant share of the final selling price. Example: The involvement of multiple middlemen in the supply chain may lead to a significant difference between the price paid by consumers and the amount received by farmers, resulting in income disparities.
b. **Lack of Post-Harvest Processing:** Insufficient post-harvest processing facilities hinder value addition to agricultural products, reducing their marketability and potential for higher returns. Example: A lack of proper processing and packaging facilities for products like grains and pulses can limit their shelf life and make them less appealing to consumers.
c. **Inefficient Market Linkages:**Weak linkages between agricultural markets and urban centers canleadtomarketinefficienciesandlimitedaccess to a broader consumer base. Example: Poor connectivity between rural and urban markets may cause fluctuations in supply and demand, leading to price volatility for both producers and consumers.**Conclusion:** Addressing these bottlenecks requires strategic policy interventions, investments in agricultural infrastructure, and the promotion of efficient market linkages. By resolving these issues, India can enhance the marketing efficiency of agricultural products, ensure better returns for farmers, and provide consumers with a steady supply of quality produce at reasonable prices

## **Decoding the Question**

The adoption of this important legislation resulted in a paradigm shift away from a welfare-based approach to food security.**Salient Features of the National Food Security Act,**

## **2013**

- **Coverage and entitlement:** With a uniform entitlement of 5 kg/person/month, up to 75% of the rural population and 50% of the urban population will be covered under TPDS.
- **Identification of households:** The task of locating eligible households must be completed by the States/UTS.
- **Nutritional support:** Pregnant women, nursing mothers and children (between the ages of six months and fourteen years) will be entitled to meals in accordance with the ICDS, MDM’s dietary standards (PM-Poshan).
- **Maternity benefit:** Maternity benefits of at least 6000 rupees are due to pregnant women and nursing mothers.
- **Women empowerment:** For the purposes of issuing ration cards, the household’s eldest woman who is at least 18 years old will be considered to be the head of the household.
- **Transparency/Accountability:** Provisions for social audits, vigilance committee formation, PDS record publication, etc.
- **Food security allowance:**In the event that the beneficiaries are not given the appropriate dietary grains or meals, they are entitled to it.**Role played by National Food Security Act in**

## **Eliminating Hunger and Malnutrition**

- In India, the number of **undernourished persons** **has decreased** by 60 million between 2006 and 2019, according to a UN report.
- The outcomes of hunger among the poor and disadvantaged have improved as a result of improved access to dietary grains.
- According to a UN report, **stunting among** **children under the age of five has fallen** from 47.8 percent in 2012 to 34.7 percent in 2019.
- **Pregnancy-related wage loss has been made up** **for financially.** PWLM now has access to a variety of fresh fruits, vegetables, and other foods.
- From 11.2 million in 2012 to 13.9 million in 2019, more infants were exclusively breastfed because of the awareness raised by the Asha workers.

## **Areas needing Improvement**

- In 2019, there will be 175.6 million women of reproductive age who are anaemic, up from 165.6 million in 2012.
- The CNNS has drawn attention to childhood hunger and malnutrition in India.
- From 25.2 million in 2012 to 34.3 million in 2016, there were more obese adults in India.
- Poor institutional infrastructure makes it difficult to implement the food bill’s requirements.
- The advantages have been diverted to middlemen and phantom beneficiaries due to pervasive corruption. Access to food grains has been revolutionised by the food bill, but we must move beyond just food security andtowardnutritionalsecurity.Further,itisimportant to use technology to address structural obstacles in the execution of the food bill.

## Question 107 (Year: 2021 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2021-gs3-q107-unacademy**
**Q14. What are the present challenges before crop diversification? How do emerging technologies provide an opportunity for crop diversification? (15 Marks, 250 Words)**

#

## Answer

**Tags: Crop Diversification**

## **Decoding the Question**

- **Introduction: Explain briefly about crop** **diversification.** -

## **Body**

- **Mention the roadblocks in crop** **diversification.**-**Highlight the role of technology in crop** **diversification.**-**Conclusion: Conclude with a way forward.** **Answer:** Crop diversification is the process of incorporating new crops or cropping systems into an existing farm’s agricultural production while taking into account the various socio-economic and environmental rewards. India has a wide variety of farming systems because of its unique range of climates, soil types, and cultures.

## **Various Roadblocks in Crop Diversification**

- **Impact of Green Revolution:** There has been a shift away from monocultures of coarse grains and toward monocultures of wheat and rice (Government policy of MSP).
- **Monsoon Dependence:** India’s cultivable land is rain-fed to the tune of about 55%, with a strong reliance on the monsoon.
- **Fragmented land holding:** It makes it challenging to employ effective contemporary technologies on a broad scale, increases the expense of managing property boundaries, causes land conflicts, etc.
- **Shift from Food crops to Commercial Crops:** Cotton in the Deccan region and sugarcane in the Green Revolution belt and Krishna-Godavari basin are two examples of this.
- **Human factors:** Subsistence farming is still practised and there is significant population pressure on the sector.
- **Infrastructural Factors:** A lack of basic infrastructure, including power, transportation, and communications in rural areas. poor post-harvest processing infrastructure is also mentioned.

## **Role of Technologies in Crop Diversification**

- **Soil and Water Sensors:** Instead of using a predetermined schedule to decide when to irrigate and fertilise, the farm can utilise these sensors to monitor moisture and nitrogen levels.
- **Weather Tracking:** Using this technology, farmers can acquire enough advance notice of hail, frost, and other weather disasters to make plans to protect their crops or, at the very least, minimise losses.
- **Satellite Imaging:** A farmer can examine crops using crop photography; even once a week photo analysis can save a farm a lot of time and money. Additionally, this technology can be used in conjunction with sensors for crops, soil, and water to give farmers alerts as well as the appropriate satellite imagery when danger thresholds are surpassed.
- **Vertical Farming:** Vertical farming, a form of urban agriculture, is the technique of growing food in layers that are piled vertically. The ability to grow in urban environments, and the resulting speedier and cheaper availability of fresher meals, is undoubtedly the most noticeable. It allows farmers from all over the world to better utilise theirlandandgrowcropsthatwouldnototherwise be possible in those regions.
- **Mini-chromosomal Technology:**Using minichromosomes, agricultural geneticists can confer dozens, if not hundreds, of traits on a plant. Two examples of complex traits are drought tolerance and nitrogen utilisation.**Way Forward** - Despite the issues that need to be resolved, crop diversification has the ability to triple farmers’ income and provide food security for the nation.
- Inordertopromotecropdiversity,thegovernment must buy crops other than wheat and rice at the MSP. Additionally, this can aid in conserving the limited subsurface water supply.
- Improved livestock management, technologyassisted fertiliser application monitoring, small field plan modifications, and other more effective agricultural practices can also cut agricultural emissions. Prioritising the preferred crops that thrive in each agroclimatic zone of the nation is urgently required in order to increase net returns for the farming community through crop diversification.

## Question 108 (Year: 2020 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2020-gs3-q108-unacademy**
**Q 3. What are the main Constraints in the transport and marketing of agricultural produce in India? (150 Words, 10 Marks) Agriculture: production and marketing Tag: , transport and marketing of agriculture produce and issues and related constraints.**

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In Introduction, try to briefly discuss** **agricultural marketing in India.**-**In Body,**-**Discuss** **main** **constraints** **in** **transportation.**-**Discuss main constraints in marketing** **goods.**-**Try to conclude by writing some suggestions.** **Answer:** India is an agriculture-dependent country and over the years agricultural produce has become significant

## **in the economy. This is evident from**

- Principal agricultural commodities export for April 2020 - January 2021 was US$ 32.12 billion.
- During the 2019-20 crop year, food grain production reached a record of 296.65 million tonnes.
- Production of horticulture crops in India was estimated at a record 319.56 million metric tonnes (MMT) in FY20.
- India is among the 15 leading exporters of agricultural products in the world. Agricultural export from India reached US$ 38.54 billion in FY19 and US$ 35.09 billion in FY20. In this context, agricultural marketing plays an important role not only in stimulating production and consumption but in accelerating the pace of economic development. The agriculture marketing system plays a dual role in economic development in countries whose resources are primarily agricultural. However,AgriculturalMarketingisoneofthemanifold problems, which have a direct bearing upon the prosperity of the cultivators. Some of the constraints are discussed below: **Constraints in the transportation of agricultural**

## **produce**

- **Poor Transportation Network:** In India, the interconnectivity between road, railway and ports are not fully developed and utilized. Thus, Accessibility between rural areas to main market centres in urban areas and various other parts of the country is poor. This results in the costly transportation of agricultural produce.
- **Lack of Pucca Roads or All-Weather Roads:** Allweather roads in rural areas is a major constraint. In monsoon season most of rural India remained disconnectedduetopoorconditionsofruralroads. Poor quality of roads leads to 16% of agricultural produce.
- **Lack of Mobile Cold Storage:** Mobile cold storage facilities are vital when it comes to the transportation of perishable agricultural produce such as vegetables, marine products, animal products etc. The lack of investment in this sector is another problem, especially private sector investment.
- **Lack of Private Investment in Storage:** Private participation in storage facilities has not come up because of the “Essential Commodities Act” as it prohibits the private sector.

## **Constraints in agricultural produce marketing**

- **Agricultural Produce Marketing Committee Act:** As per the act, farmers have to sell their produce in designated markets and designated places. This compulsion makes farmers sell their produce at a distressed price and he could not sell his produce in any other market which resulted in the exploitation of farmers.
- **Inaccessible Information** on future pricing, inadequate information regarding marketing mechanisms etc. leads to the exploitation of farmers by the middlemen.
- **Too Many Middlemen:** There are too many middlemen in the channel of distribution between the wholesaler or the miller in the producing end and the wholesaler at the consuming end.
- **Absence of Grading:** The absence of grading and standardisation of agricultural produce is another great stumbling block hindering the growth of markets and smooth marketing operations.
- **Absence of Regulated Markets:** All markets and market yards are not regulated. There are more than14,000marketsspreadovertheentirecountry. Most of the wholesale mandis are regulated but primary or local markets operating in the villages and small towns are still unregulated.
- **Absence of Co-Operative Marketing:** The farmers are still reluctant to pool their produce and allow a cooperative organisation to sell the pooled and graded produce. The development of co-operative marketing got the tempo only after 1960. The growth is relatively slow.

## **Way Forward**

- **Integrating Agri-Markets:** The Government has announced an E-NAM project to connect all the wholesale markets through the pan-India trading market. But there are still issues of internet connectivity, there is no evidence of the reduced role of middlemen in these marketplaces. These issues must be addressed to make this programme successful and achieve its desired objectives.
- **Promotion of Farmers Producers Organization:** It will help farmers on a large scale by increasing competitive bidding for farmers’ produce and giving the best possible price for their agricultural produce. So, it is imperative to promote the Farmer Producer Organizations as it will also help in achieving the targets of doubling the farmer’s income.
- **Legislative Reforms:** legislative reforms need to be taken especially in essential commodities acts, APMC acts, and all those legislative measures need to be taken which help the farming sector to achieve its potential growth by considering all the stakeholders.
- **Kisan Rail:**It has been very successful during the pandemic; it has brought much-needed relief to the farming community to solve the issue of marketing and transportation of agricultural produce in various parts of the country. Now it is high time to increase Kisan rail routes and connect every part of the country and make available the whole country as a market for farmers and create**“One Country One Agriculture Market”.**Thus, to achieve the target of doubling farmers income and accelerating the agriculture growth rate, it is necessary to solve issues related to transportation and agricultural produce marketing and make farming communities and villages self-sufficient or**“gram** **swaraj”.** ---

## Question 110 (Year: 2020 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2020-gs3-q110-unacademy**
**Q13. What are the major factors responsible for making rice-wheat system a success? In spite of this success how has this system become bane in India? (250 Words 15 Marks) Tag: Major crops, cropping patterns in various parts of the country -different types of irrigation system storage, transport and marketing of agriculture produce and issues and related constraints, e-technology in the aid of farmers.**

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In Introduction, try to write about the rice-** **wheat system.**-**In Body,**-**Discuss factors responsible for making** **the rice-wheat system a success.**-**Discuss how this system is responsible** **for creating issues/bane.**-**Try to conclude with a wayforward.**
**Answer:**The Green Revolution revolutionised rice and wheat production in the india. India, now is one of the leading producers in rice and wheat production in the world. Rice is one of the important kharif crops and wheat is one of the rabi crops in the country. Both, the rice-wheat system is the cornerstone of India’s food self-sufficiency. There are many factors that can be attributed to the successful production of Rice and wheat in the country.**Factors responsible for making rice-wheat system a**

##**success**

-**Improved Technologies and access to same:**Technologies played a very important role in the rise of the rice-wheat system.

- Important role in success of green revolution and introduction of HYV seeds, zero tillage, bed planting, direct seeding etc Improved production of wheat and rice and responsible for making the rice-wheat system a success. Later on, the same seeds became accessible for all farming communities.
-**Efficient use of machinery:**Though the level of mechanisation is very high, the mechanisation of agriculture has been increasing over a period of time. Use of harvesters, tractors, crop harvesting machinery etc. has**improved agricultural** **productivityandlossofcropdamageascompared** to traditional methods of crop harvesting.

- **Improved methods of irrigation:** The prerequisite for success of the green revolution, which focuses on increasing production of rice and wheat, is irrigation methods. The development of dense network Canal irrigation, tubewells as well as methods such as sprinklers, drip irrigation, canals etc made it possible to grow rice and wheat in areas of less rainfall such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.
- **New crop varieties:** Impetus to Research and Development in agriculture has improved Seeds Varieties of rice and wheat.
- **Fertilisers:** Use of Neem coated urea and biofertilizers improved the production of wheat and rice systems.
- **Organic farming:** It is a new concept gaining ground in agriculture because of the rising level of demand for organic foods in the market. It is also being followed in production of wheat, rice. Though this system improved wheat and rice production and increased country’s food production to the level of export of these item, it has created some serious issues,
- **Declining Groundwater Table:** Rice is a water intensive crop, and it requires a lot of water to take rice crops in a year. The rice- wheat system has largely been responsible for the declining groundwater table in areas of Haryana, Punjab etc (areas under green revolution) which created ecological issues and made farming activity unsustainable.
- **Excessive Use of Pesticide:** Excessive use of pesticideshascreatedproblemsforpollinatorssuch as bees, bottle flies and important microorganisms under soils severely impacted due excessive use of pesticides. This also leads to the problem of algal bloom and destruction of the lake ecosystem.
- **Burning of Crop Residues:** Farmers do not have technologies to turn agricultural residues into fertilizers and convert them into useful bio fertilizers. They burn these crop residues which severely pollute the air in cities like Delhi, which are becoming main reasons for respiratory problems and various heart related issues.
- **Degradation of Soil:** Due to increased demand of rice and wheat farmers are taking 2 to 3 crops in year which results in exhausting soil nutrients, both macro and micro, and these nutrients are compensated through excessive fertilizers use, and soils are becoming saline further increasing desertification etc.
- **Weed Management:** To kill unwanted weeds and to keep nutrients supplied even for crops, farmers are using various chemical based solutions for weed management which is killing important organisms such as earthworms. It also becomes a quality issue of food when it comes to export of agricultural produce. Though the rice-wheat system has solved the food problem and made India from a food deficient country to food surplus country. But it has created several issues which need to be addressed to make the rice wheat system production sustainable. It is the need of the hour to implement the recommendations given by the National Farmers’ Commission under the leadership of M.S. Swaminathan which aims to make agriculture a source of income and employment along with a comprehensive and sustainable shift in agricultural practices.

## Question 111 (Year: 2019 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

**Question ID: 2019-gs3-q111-unacademy**
**Q 3. How far is the Integrated Farming System (IFS) helpful in sustaining agricultural production? (150 Words 10 Marks) Tag: Major Crops - Cropping Patterns in various partsofthecountry,-DifferentTypesofIrrigation and Irrigation Systems; Storage, Transport and Marketing of Agricultural Produce and Issues and Related Constraints.**

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In Introduction, try to define Integrated** **Farming System (IFS).**-**In Body,**-**Enlist goals of IFS.**-**ElaboratehowIFSishelpfulinsustaining** **agricultural production.**-**Mention some of the challenges** **associated with it.**-**Try to conclude with suggestions and** **significance of IFS.** **Answer:**Integrated Farming System (IFS) is an**interdependent** **and interrelated production system**based on a few crops, animals and related subsidiary enterprises to maximize the utilization of nutrients of each system and minimize the negative effect of these enterprises on the environment. The nature of IFS involves the utilization of primary produce and secondary produce of one system, as basic input of the other system, thus making them mutually integrated as one whole unit.**Examples** of IFS include - Integrated Fish cum Pig farming, Integrated Fish Farming-Chicken, Integrated Fish farming-cum-Agriculture etc.

## **Major goals of IFS are**

- Maximization of yield for stable income.
- Achieve agro-ecological equilibrium.
- Controlling insects-pest, diseases and weeds.
- Reducing the use of agro-chemical inputs.
- Mitigation of negative impact of agriculture or livestock on the environment.

## **IFS and Sustained Agricultural Production**

- **Increased Farm Income:** Through proper residue recycling and allied components and preparing manure which can be again used for organic farming. IFS also increases the yield of farming.
- **Income Stability:** Regular stable income through theproductslikeegg,milk,mushroom,vegetables, honey, and silkworm cocoons from the linked activities in integrated farming. Stability in income can help in boosting rural agricultural entrepreneurship.
- **Sustainable Soil Fertility:** Organic waste recycling helps to reduce problems of burning of farm residue and increase soil fertility sustainably.
- **Increased Nutrition:** Integration of allied activities will result in the availability of nutritious food enriched with protein, carbohydrate, fat, minerals, and vitamins.
- **Environment Protection:** Integrated farming will help in environmental protection through effective recycling of waste from animal activities like piggery, poultry, and pigeon rearing.
- **Agriculture and Allied Activities:** Cultivation of fodder crops as intercropping and as border cropping will result in the availability of adequate nutritious fodder for animal components like milch cow, goat / sheep, pig and rabbit.
- **Agroforestry:** Firewood and construction wood requirements could be met from the agroforestry system without affecting the natural forest.
- Avoidance of soil loss through erosion by Agro-forestry and proper cultivation of each part of land by integrated farming.
- **On Farm Employment Generation:** Generation of regular employment for the farm family members of small and marginal farmers. This will help to reduce distressed migration among rural populations during droughts and other times.
- **To Feed Increasing Population:** Higher food production to equate the demand of the exploding population of our nation.

## **Some Challenges**

- **Financial Support:** This can be a gamechanger for small and marginal farmers if financial support is available.
- **Lack of Awareness:** Most of the farmers are not aware of the benefits of IFS and extension services.
- **Wheat-Rice Dominance:** Mainly due to Minimum Support Prices farmers are hesitant for transition to IFS. Therefore,promotingtheIntegratedFarmingSystemis a vital and prominent solution for various agricultural problemsespeciallyfarmer’sdistressandimprovingthe agrarian economy. It is high time that the government should promote and include farming communities in adopting IFS on a large-scale basis.

## **Security**

## Question 114 (Year: 2017 | Paper: GS III | Marks: 10)

#

## Answer

## **Decoding the Question**

- **In Intro, try to define the cropping system** **and highlight the declining trend of rice and** **wheat crops yields.**-**In Body,**-**Discuss the reasons for the declining** **trend of rice and wheat yield.**-**Discussthemeritsofcropdiversification.**-**Try to conclude by linking with the** **Sustainable Development Goals.** **Answer:** A cropping system is the type and sequence of crops grown and practices used for growing them. In India rice and wheat is the dominant cropping system. Rice and wheat cropping system is - water, capital, labor and energy intensive and become less profitable as these resources diminish. According to the Economic Survey 2015-16 yields of major crops like paddy and

## **wheat are declining**

- In wheat, India’s average yield in 2013 of 3075 kg/ ha is lower than the world average of 3257 kg/ha.
- In paddy production, all Indian states have yields below that of China and most states have yields below that of Bangladesh.
- India’s best state, Punjab, has paddy yield close to 6000 kg/ha whereas China’s yield is 6709 kg/ha.

## **Reasonsbehinddecliningyieldsofriceandwheatare**

- **Declining Soil Fertility:** Excessive use of nutrients and use of flood irrigation system the soil in paddy and wheat producing areas has become saline and losing its fertility. Decreased soil fertility and increasing demand created a lot of pressure on limited agricultural land, this led to excessive use of inputs like fertilizers, faulty irrigation practices etc.
- **Increased Cost of Inputs:** Inputs such as seeds, labour cost, newer machines, fertilizers costs transportation cost etc. has been constantly increasing which made cultivation of rice and wheat cultivation costly affair.
- **Climate Change:** Changing climate made the monsoon unpredictable. Climate change has adversely impacted the yield of crops like wheat, rice etc.
- **Changing Groundwater:** Over-exploitation of ground water led to declining groundwater table. Declining groundwater table becoming unsustainable for such crops.
- **Poor Crop Diversification:** Due to Minimum Support Price farmers are increasingly producing wheat and rice this made farmers are not give emphasis on crop diversification. Poor practice of crop diversification is largely responsible for declining soil nutrients and productivity. Government has increasingly created awareness against domination practices of wheat and rice sowing. Government also making policies for crop diversification and people are becoming conscious about nutrition and accordingly they are changing their food habits. Therefore it is imperative to focus on crop diversification. Crop diversification refers to the shift from regional dominance of one crop to production number of crops. Crop diversification helps in

## **following manner**

- Declining **Arrest Declining Groundwater:** groundwatercanbestoppedbycropdiversification. Growingcropsaccordingtotheclimaticconditions and available water resources will definitely help in arresting declining groundwater sources.
- **Increase Soil Nutrients:** Crops such as pulses, coarse grains are known as hardy crops as they can grow in less nutrient and less water available areas. These crops even help in fixing nitrogen in soil which is one of the very essential components for crops growth.
- **Nutritional Security:** Dependent on wheat and rice will create a challenge of nutritional security. India is having one of the largest populations with malnutrition and micronutrients deficiency. Crop diversification will help in solving these issues.
- **Soil Biodiversity:** Crop diversity helps in maintaining soil biodiversity. This soil biodiversity is very essential for crops survival as they keep on recycling soil nutrients.
- **Increasing Tolerance:** With crop diversification the crops in drier areas can be clubbed with the less water consuming crops like millets. India, being a vast country, has wide variations in agro climatic conditions. Such variations have led to the evolution of regional niches for various crops. Therefore, single domination of one cropping system needs to be rejected. The government is promoting cropdiversificationingreenrevolutionareasofPunjab, Haryana and western UP to reduce negative impacts on soil from rice and wheat cultivation. This is a necessary step to achieve the sustainable development goal to ensure zero hunger.
